pll1d28c2-d1e3501.summary: Asks whether, as only the Father is called unbegotten, he alone should be called not-begotten or not-son, so the Spirit could not be.

pll1d28c2-d1e3506.summary: Reports one opinion: only the Father should be called not-begotten or not-son; the Spirit, as not unbegotten, should not be called 'not-begotten' or 'not-son,' though he should be said not to be begotten or a son.
claims: On this view only the Father is 'not-begotten.'

pll1d28c2-d1e3510.summary: Reports another opinion: the Spirit cannot be called unbegotten but can be called not-begotten or not-son; Augustine's equation was said to show the etymology of the name, not the rule of predication.
claims: On this view the Spirit can be called 'not-begotten.'
Augustine spoke of etymology, not predication.

pl-l1d28c2.summary: Asks whether, as the Father alone is unbegotten, he alone should be called 'not-begotten' or 'not-son,' so that the Spirit could not be. Some say the Spirit should be said not to be begotten or a son, but not to be 'not-begotten' or 'not-son.' Others say the Spirit, though not 'unbegotten,' can be called 'not-begotten' or 'not-son,' and that Augustine's equation referred to etymology, not predication.
claims: Some hold that only the Father should be called not-begotten or not-son.
They allow that the Spirit is not begotten, but not that he is 'not-begotten.'
Others hold the Spirit can be called not-begotten or not-son, though not unbegotten.
On that view Augustine's equation of 'unbegotten' and 'not-begotten' concerns etymology, not predication.
